analysis.one_liner: Bans employers and health insurers from using people's genetic information against them.
analysis.headline: The Genetic Privacy and Nondiscrimination Act of 1995 died in a Senate committee without ever receiving a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made a person's genetic information private by default: no one could disclose it without that person's specific written permission, except for narrow purposes like criminal investigations or court orders. It would have banned employers from requiring genetic tests or using genetic information to discriminate against workers, with remedies under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and barred health insurers from using genetic information to deny, cancel, limit, or raise the price of coverage. It also asked the National Bioethics Advisory Commission to recommend rules for storing and using DNA samples.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose genes suggest a future illness — people with family histories of cancer, Huntington's disease, sickle cell trait, and other inherited conditions. The bill would have stopped employers from screening them out of jobs and health insurers from rejecting them, canceling their policies, or charging them more based on their DNA. It also would have given everyone a say over who sees their genetic information, since DNA reveals things about parents, siblings, and children too.

how_it_helps.text: Bars employers from seeking, obtaining, or using an employee's or job applicant's genetic information, or requiring a genetic test, to discriminate against them or restrict any right or benefit — enforced through the same powers and remedies as the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Prohibits health insurers from using genetic information to reject, deny, limit, cancel, refuse to renew, or raise rates on coverage, so a person's DNA could not be used to price them out of health insurance.

Makes genetic information confidential by default: no entity could disclose it, or be compelled to disclose it by subpoena, without the individual's specific written authorization naming what is disclosed, to whom, and why — with narrow exceptions for criminal justice, court orders, paternity, telling close relatives of a deceased person for diagnosis, and identifying bodies.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and health insurers, who would lose the ability to use genetic test results to screen out workers or applicants likely to run up medical costs. Life and other non-health insurers would face lighter new requirements: they could still require genetic tests but would have to tell applicants how results would be used and get written authorization to disclose them.

drawbacks.text: The bill left life, disability, and other non-health insurance largely untouched: those insurers could still require a genetic test as a condition of coverage, needing only to disclose how results would be used and obtain written authorization to share them. Genetic discrimination in those markets would have continued.

It did not decide the hardest questions — how DNA samples may be collected, stored, and retained — and instead deferred to a National Bioethics Advisory Commission report due by August 31, 1996, leaving current practices in place in the meantime.

Its broad exceptions allowed genetic information to be disclosed for criminal or death investigations, juvenile proceedings, child fatality reviews, and paternity cases, and the ban on compelled disclosure by subpoena applied only outside those exceptions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections were real and addressed a harm that was growing as genetic testing spread: without a law, a person's DNA could cost them a job or their health coverage. The costs fell on employers and insurers in the form of lost screening power and compliance burdens, which is precisely the point of the bill. The honest criticism is that the bill was incomplete — it shielded health insurance but left life and disability insurers free to test and price by genes, and it punted on DNA sample storage to a future commission report. A stronger bill would have closed those gaps; this one was a starting framework.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no further action until Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Hatfield introduced the bill on November 15, 1995, together with Senator Connie Mack, and spoke about it on the Senate floor the same day.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources that day — the standard first step that sends a bill to the committee with jurisdiction over it.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action. When the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers, who could keep using genetic information to screen workers and applicants; more than a decade passed before Congress enacted a federal genetic nondiscrimination law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers that screen by genes

for.name: Sen. Mark Hatfield
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Connie Mack
for.what_they_did: Joined Hatfield in introducing the bill.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only three senators ever supported the bill on the record — two Republicans and one Democrat — and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of the opposition was never revealed.

industries.note: The bill barred health insurers from using genetic information to reject, deny, limit, cancel, refuse to renew, or raise rates on coverage. Their interest in screening out people whose genes predict expensive care ran directly against the people the bill protected.

The bill prohibited employers from requiring genetic tests or using genetic information in employment decisions, with Civil Rights Act remedies for workers. Employers could no longer use DNA to sort job applicants and employees by predicted medical cost.

The bill left their core practice intact: they could still require a genetic test as a condition of coverage. It added only a duty to tell applicants how results would be used and to obtain written authorization before disclosing them.
